title: Koivun moves 3 strokes up at the 3M Open with a 3rd-round 61 and tournament-record back 9
description: PGA Tour rookie Jackson Koivun shot a 61 in the third round of the 3M Open to take a three-stroke lead at 20-under par.
fullText:
BLAINE, Minn. (AP) — PGA Tour rookie Jackson Koivun shot a 61 in the third round of the 3M Open on Saturday to take a three-stroke lead at 20-under par, setting a tournament record with a 28 on the back nine at the TPC Twin Cities.

Emiliano Grillo and Ben Kohles each had a 65 and are tied for second at 17 under. Michael Brennan shot a 63 and shared fourth with Chandler Phillips at 16 under. Denny McCarthy, Billy Horschel and Michael Kim were in sixth at 15 under.

Scottie Scheffler, the world’s top-ranked player, was six strokes behind Koivun in a four-way tie for ninth place with Davis Thompson, Seamus Power and Brian Harman.

The 21-year-old Koivun, who was the top-ranked amateur player after a standout college career at Auburn and turned pro last month following the U.S. Open, had two eagles and six birdies to separate from the pack on a steamy and still afternoon that was ideal for low scores.

“Just got to keep the foot on the gas,” Koivun said.

Koivun sank a 12-foot putt on the 12th green and a 14-footer on the 18th to eagle two of the three par-5s on the lake-filled course, which joined the tour schedule in 2019. He confidently hit his second shot from the 18th fairway over the water and landed safely on the green.

“It’s going to be definitely a test tomorrow,” Koivun said. “I’m sure some of the pins will be tucked and we’ve got a lot of great players behind me, but just going to stick to my game plan and try to smile.”

Koivun, who tied for 10th two weeks ago at the ISCO Championship in Kentucky, shot a 64 on Thursday and a 68 on Friday. He tied the 54-hole record (193) set by wire-to-wire 2023 champion Lee Hodges and became the youngest 54-hole leader on tour this season. But don’t assume he’s a stranger to this type of pressure.

“Playing at Auburn was so much fun. We were definitely put in some stressful situations at national championships and just collegiate play,” Koivun said. “I’m just trying to lean on those experiences.”

Kohles, who shot a 62 for the first-round lead, went bogey-free in pursuit of his first tour victory. Grillo, the 33-year-old Argentine, eagled the 18th to make up for some earlier putting misses.

“These kids are playing better every day,” Grillo said. “It’s hard to keep up with them. I’ve just got to go and shoot my lowest.”

Scheffler had an eagle and five birdies on the back nine, but his afternoon wasn’t all that special. Three others matched his 64, and four players went lower than that.

Bringing a big gallery with him to watch every shot, with fans packed several rows deep along the ropes, Scheffler had the crowd going wild when he eagled the 16th by sinking a 55-footer on the par-4 hole.

“The support this week’s been tremendous. The crowd here has been great not only to myself but to the guys who’ve been playing well,” Scheffler said.

Kim, who took a three-stroke lead into the weekend with a second-round 59 that made him the 15th player in tour history to go below 60, lost his touch with the putter and finished with a 70.

“I’m really happy with the way I swung it today. I was pleasantly surprised at how calm I was feeling heading to the first tee,” Kim said. “Overall, I’m pretty happy with it, but a little disappointed that I’m five back.”

title: A pretty pleasant afternoon
description: Lee hit a 3-run homer, Devers hit a 3-run homer, no leads were lost, solid day.
fullText:
July has been tough on Jung Hoo Lee.

Tough, especially after a June in which he hit .340 with an .858 OPS and peaked with a two hit night against the Athletics that raised his batting average to a season high .333 on June 23rd. Knocks were coming off his bat like water from a hose. Grounders found holes, flares frolicked in open fields, liners hugged the lines. But for many high contact, low hard-hit guys like Lee the spigot can close just as easily as it can open. The seventh month wasn’t so lucky.

Over 67 at-bats prior to Saturday, he hit just .224 with a .541 OPS. Last night’s 0-for-4 performance saw his batting average drop below the .300 mark for the first time since May 31st. In his first at-bat against Angels’ starter Ryan Johnson, Lee seemed like a completely different person to the hitter he was during his 18-game hitting streak. The right-hander’s two-step motion and sling-y delivery had him flailing. He unhinged a swing on an elevated 2-1 sweeper and the bat nearly flew out of his hands. Next pitch, his helmet flew off whiffing at an inside cutter. Grandson of the Wind? More like Generator of the Wind! It’s jokes like that which made Lee into one of the greatest hitters in recent KBO history. He had had enough. His typically stoic expression turned stony as he walked back to the dugout. It wasn’t the missed cutter that irked him — that was a good pitch — but the breaking ball, lazily flipped out over the plate. Instead of getting off his best swing, he nearly ripped his shoulder out of his socket. That was unacceptable.

An inning later, the offense had Johnson on the ropes. The inherent funk of his motion had bought him a free pass first time through the order, but once the line-up flipped back over for second licks, the situation had changed.

Both Luis Arraez and Heliot Ramos singled. With runners at the corners and one out, Johnson got Eldridge to strikeout, but didn’t have the same success against Rafael Devers and Casey Schmitt. Back-to-back RBI singles got the Giants on the scoreboard and encouraged LA pitching coach Mike Maddux to chat with the 23 year old starter.

The transcript from mound visit probably went something like this: Hey, man, deep breath, you’re doing fine, just take a deep breath, calm down, one more out and you’re through this inning, just trust your stuff, stick to your game plan, don’t over think anything, stick to your game plan, okay, trust the preparation, you know what you got to do, remember how bad Lee looked  on that sweeper in the last at-bat, jumping out of his shoes, he looked like s*** swinging at that thing, grandson of the wind, more like generator of the wind, haha, like a fan, yeah, so do that again, that’s the game plan,he’s not looking for your breaking ball, you stole a strike with it to start the at-bat, you made him look bad with it for strike two, then you got him with the cutter, pitch him backwards, start with the sweeper, throw that sweeper, trust it, it’ll be awesome, okay, the umpire is coming so I gotta go, you’re gonna do great, I’m so proud of you, sweeper, throw it, okay, see you in a bit, bye.

The takeaway for Johnson: Throw the sweeper because my coach says so and he believes in me.

What happened: Johnson threw the sweeper. First pitch. Lee knew he would.

The 3-run homer was Lee’s sixth of the year, his first since June 23rd, and jump-started a pretty dang pleasant afternoon. He collected a double off lefty reliever Brent Suter in his next at-bat, tracked down an over-the-head liner to end the 4th, and recorded a Dolly Parton assist (9-5) in the 6th.

Lee wasn’t the only one who enjoyed their day. The deliverer of walk-offs, Rafael Devers, came up a triple shy of the cycle. He picked up Eldridge after his strikeout with a 2-out RBI single in the 3rd, and with two outs again, he ripped a gorgeous line-drive over the wall in left-center.

A 106 MPH punch like that is not something Suter gives up often. His 29.8% hard-hit rate is in the 95th percentile of pitchers. Like Tyler Rogers, he’s a master of dead-fish contact. He’s also a lefty, and for whatever reason, Devers has been completely baffled by southpaws in 2026. Before his homer, he was batting .181 with .530 OPS and a 49 wRC+, which is about as ineffective as you can get in that split. For most of the at-bat, right up until the end, that season-long struggle was evident. Devers waved over two of Suter’s slow-mo change-ups, and fouled off another with an awkward emergency swing. He didn’t look particularly comfortable at the plate. Suter could’ve kept spinning that offspeed, and eventually, Devers would’ve swung through one — but the reliever decided to get cute and tried to sneak a 90 MPH four-seam fastball by him. Devers clocked it and then CLOCKED it.

Another three-run swing that pumped up the lead to 9 runs, putting the game out of reach of Los Angeles bats and more importantly, Giants relievers. While the offense efficiently piled up 9 runs on 9 hits over the first four frames, starter Robbie Ray quietly went about his business. The extended time on the bench between halves didn’t bother him. He wasn’t dominant, nor was he batted around. Five of the six hits he scattered across his six shutout innings were singles. He needed just 80 pitches before Tony Vitello elected to give Tristan Beck and eventually Keaton Winn some low-leverage, no-pressure reps.

It wasn’t pretty, nor did it look easy at times — they walked three, hit a batter, gave up three hits and two runs, but they got through it.

title: Guardians score vs. Rays. Slumping Cleveland shut out by Tampa Bay
description: Nick Martinez tossed six shutout innings, Yandy Diaz recorded a milestone hit and the Rays beat the Guardians on July 25 in St. Petersburg, Fla.
fullText:
Nick Martinez tossed six shutout innings and Yandy Diaz recorded his 1,000th career hit with Tampa Bay as the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-0 on Saturday, July 25, in St. Petersburg, Fla.

Martinez (10-2) allowed four singles with no walks and five strikeouts. He has allowed three earned runs or fewer in 19 of his 20 starts this season.

Cole Sulser and Garrett Cleavinger each pitched a scoreless inning before Bryan Baker worked around a one-out single in the ninth for his 27th save.

Chandler Simpson and Diaz, who started his career in Cleveland, had two hits apiece for Tampa Bay, which recorded its seventh shutout and won for the fifth time in its last six games.

Diaz lined a leadoff single to right field in the first inning against Tanner Bibee (4-10) to become the fourth player in franchise history to record 1,000 hits with the team.

Cleveland lost its fourth consecutive game and has scored a total of four runs in its last three.

Tampa Bay threatened to move ahead with the bases loaded and two outs in the fourth inning, but Bibee escaped unscathed on Ben Williamson's groundout.

The Rays broke the scoreless tie in the fifth. Diaz hit a one-out double and moved to third on Jonathan Aranda's single before scoring on Junior Caminero's double off the right-field wall. Cedric Mullins followed with a sacrifice fly to put Tampa Bay ahead 2-0.

With runners on the corners and one out in the sixth, the Rays added to their lead when Victor Mesa Jr. scored on Hunter Feduccia's sacrifice bunt.

Bibee yielded three runs on nine hits over six innings. He walked two and struck out five while throwing a season-high 107 pitches.

title: Report: NFLPA investigating Panthers for possible CBA violation. Here's why
description: The NFL Players Association is investigating the Carolina Panthers for the circumstances surrounding Nic Scourton's recent ACL tear.
fullText:
The NFL Players Association is investigating the Carolina Panthers.

According to Joe Person of The Athletic, the NFLPA plans to examine the circumstances surrounding second-year edge rusher Nic Scourton's injury. Scourton tore his ACL on the first day of Panthers training camp, on Thursday, July 23.

Per Person, the NFLPA will be looking into whether the Panthers were following the rules of an acclimation period to begin training camp that are laid out in the league and union's Collective Bargaining Agreement. The CBA's guidelines state that live contact is prohibited during the first five days of training camp, and that the first day of camp "shall be limited to physical examinations, meetings, and classroom instruction; no on-field activities shall be permitted other than running and conditioning."

NIC SCOURTON: Panthers LB carted off with knee injury at training camp. Latest updates

The NFLPA's investigation will determine whether the Panthers were following protocol and if Scourton's injury was of a non-contact variety. If they review the video of Carolina's practice and determine otherwise, the team could face punishment for violating the CBA.

Scourton, 21, was a second-round pick by the Panthers in the 2025 NFL Draft. As a rookie last year, he appeared in all 17 games, starting eight of them, and recorded five sacks. Heading into 2026, Scourton was set for a potential breakout year playing alongside Carolina's top-flight free agent linebacker signings: Jaelan Phillips and Devin Lloyd. Instead, he likely will miss all of the 2026 season with a torn ACL.

title: Quieter night in pool for Scots, but more finals reached
description: No podium places or rousing renditions of Flower of Scotland at Tollcross on Saturday night, but the home swimming ranks still have cause for cheer.
fullText:
Friday night at Tollcross was always going to be a tough act to follow, eh?

There were no podium places or rousing renditions of Flower of Scotland on Saturday night, but there was still cause for smiles among the Team Scotland swimming ranks, with more spots in finals secured.

The roar which rippled round here when Duncan Scott tapped the wall at the end of the men's 200m individual medley final will struggle to be matched, but the loudest cheer on this night came when Angharad Evans stormed to victory in the second semi-final of the women's 100m breaststroke.

The 23-year-old is a frightening prospect in the pool and made everyone sit up - if they weren't already - as she cantered home to book her place in Sunday's final with the fastest time.

That showpiece is at 19:20 BST. One hour later, Katie Shanahan will be searching for her second medal following Friday's silver in the 200m backstroke, in the 100m backstroke final after finishing fourth in her semi-final.

Scott overcomes pressure and big pal Dean to give Scotland golden start

Shanahan missed the chance for a second chunk of metal in the last race of the night as she competed in the 4x100m mixed relay team who finished fifth, though they did set a new Scottish record.

Part of the team was, surprisingly, poster boy Scott.

He received a hero's welcome as he returned, racing second after Evan Jones and before Evie Davies, but ultimately the field was too strong.

Earlier in the evening, Sean McCann finished eighth in the men’s 400m freestyle final, Lucy Grieve was seventh in the women's 50m butterfly final and Matthew Ward broke the men’s 50m backstroke Scottish record on his way to seventh in that final.

title: Nowacki beats Ramsay-Peaty to land Jersey's first Games medal in 36 years
description: Swimmer Filip Nowacki wins Jersey's first Commonwealth Games medal in 36 years after taking silver in the 100m breaststroke.
fullText:
Swimmer Filip Nowacki has won Jersey's first Commonwealth Games medal in 36 years after taking silver in the 100m breaststroke.

The 18-year-old, who is the world junior 100m and 200m breaststroke champion, finished second behind Australia's Sam Williamson by 0.17 seconds with world record-holder Adam Ramsay-Peaty 0.31 seconds behind him in third.

Nowacki was fourth going into the turn at 50m but put in a superb second 50m leg to overtake Ramsay-Peaty and the early leader South Africa's Michael Houlie.

"I'm really happy with that swim," Nowacki told BBC Jersey.

"It was just a touch outside my personal best, but it's a true privilege racing Adam, the Aussies and the very best in the world in a senior environment."

The teenager has more chances for medals later in the week as he aims to become the most decorated Jersey athlete at the Commonwealth Games - the highest level islanders can compete at under their own flag.

He will race against mentor and world record-holder Ramsay-Peaty in the 50m breaststroke which starts on Sunday.

Nowacki's best chance of winning gold looks to be in the 200m breaststroke which begins on Tuesday - he is the reigning British champion and is the fastest qualifier for the event.

"It gives me confidence going forwards," he added.

"But it's not given that my 200's going to be great, so it's just about focusing in on the 200 now and the 50 tomorrow.

"I love getting my hand on the wall and top three bringing back some silverware and I'm very happy with that."

Ramsay-Peaty in tears after missing out on gold again

Having grown up on an island with about 100,000 inhabitants, Nowacki is rapidly become one of the best breaststrokers in the world.

He left Jersey to train at Millfield School and will move to Loughborough after the Games to continue his swimming as part of Team GB's elite squad preparing for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

Nathan Jegou, who coached Nowacki as a youngster and is managing the Jersey swimming team in Glasgow, says he is excited at what the islander can do.

"It's just the start of his journey, and the last two years for him has been phenomenal," he told BBC Jersey.

"I'm excited to see what he does and we're proud that he's one of us.

"We're such a small island, to come here and get a silver medal, it means everything to him, means everything to us, and we hope he can maybe do it again later in the week."

Nowacki becomes just the fifth person to ever win a Commonwealth Games medal while representing Jersey.

The last time Jersey made it onto the podium was in 1990 when Colin Mallett won the island's only gold medal in fullbore shooting, before teaming up with his father Cliff to win pairs bronze.

Four years earlier, bantamweight boxer John Sillitoe won bronze in Edinburgh, while Jersey's first-ever medal was also in the ring when Albert Turmel won welterweight bronze in Perth in 1962.

Islanders have won medals for England - diver Dot Macready won 10m gold in 1934, while more recently Serena Guthrie was part of the England team that won netball gold in 2018.

In 2006 Rebecca Herbert was part of the England hockey team that won bronze, while there were two bronze medals in 2002 for islanders representing England - Elizabeth Cann in badminton and swimmer Simon Militis in the 200m backstroke.

With two more events to go, Nowacki has the chance to equal Colin Mallett as the only islander to win two medals.

But at the age of 18 who would bet against the swimmer going on to become the most decorated Commonwealth Games athlete in Jersey's history?

title: Wales claim two swimming medals on dramatic night
description: Wales claim two more Commonwealth Games medals in the pool with Para-swimmer Rhys Darbey and the 4x100m mixed freestyle relay squad winning bronze in Glasgow.
fullText:
Wales claimed two more Commonwealth Games medals in the pool with Para-swimmer Rhys Darbey and the 4x100m mixed freestyle relay squad winning bronze in Glasgow.

Darbey, the 19-year-old from Deeside, initially finished fourth in the men's S14 200m freestyle final after being edged out by team-mate and room-mate Dylan Broom.

But Broom was agonisingly disqualified for "initiating a start early", which meant Darbey was promoted to third.

Olympic champion Matt Richards won the first Commonwealth Games medal of his career as part of the relay squad alongside Dan Jones, Rebecca Sutton and Theodora Taylor.

Darbey and the relay squad have followed fellow Welsh Para-swimmer Ela Letton-Jones onto the podium after she claimed silver on the opening night, with Team Wales' tally now standing at three.

Wales at the Commonwealth Games

With four fourth places in Birmingham in 2022, Richards was competing in his first event in Glasgow and looking for his first Commonwealth medal to complete the set of Olympic, world and European podium positions.

Wales opted for an entirely different quartet in the pool in the final after Kieran Bird, Harry Milne, Medi Harris and Meghan Higgs had qualified fourth fastest in the heats.

Sutton and Taylor had qualified for their respective individual semi-finals in the 100m backstroke and 100m breaststroke, but both pulled out with a full focus on the relay.

The policy paid off and Taylor, 17, brought Wales back from fifth to third with a brilliant final leg.

"A lot of training has gone into a swim like that and you don't see the hours of training that we've all put in behind the scenes," said Taylor.

"So to come out like that with success, is amazing. It's great to be able to represent my country with this amazing team."

Sutton added: "It's just an insane feeling. Like, all the adrenaline still pumping now.

"I'm just so proud of everyone, all the guys that were in the heat and bringing us through to the final for us to set it up and get our medal."

Jones was just glad to get on the podium.

"I'm over the moon," said Jones.

"From the Games last time with four fourth places, as soon as I finished them, I knew I wanted four more years because I knew this team is capable of getting on that podium."

Earlier, Rose Williams finished fourth in the women's S14 200m freestyle final.

The S14 category covers swimmers who have an intellectual impairment, which typically leads to the athletes having difficulties with regard to pattern recognition, sequencing, and memory, or having a slower reaction time, which impact on sport performance in general.

Tyler Melbourne-Smith finished sixth in the 400m freestyle final, while Lewis Fraser qualified for the 100m butterfly final to be staged on Sunday evening.

title: Leigh keep rolling with win over rivals Warrington
description: Leigh Leopards make it five straight wins with a strong 28-12 success over fellow play-off contenders Warrington Wolves.
fullText:
Tries: Armstrong, Lam, Senior, Ofahengaue, Hanley Goals: Cook 4

Tries: Sipley, Hopoate Goals: Irwin 2

Leigh Leopards made it five successive victories as they out-muscled fellow play-off contenders Warrington Wolves.

Victory moved Leigh up one place to fifth, above last year's champions Hull KR, and now level on points with the Wolves, who suffered a third defeat in four matches this month.

Early tries from David Armstrong and Lachlan Lam gave the Leopards control and they never really relinquished it.

Toafofoa Sipley crossed for Warrington but further tries from Innes Senior, Joe Ofahengaue and Umyla Hanley either side of the break moved the hosts out of sight before a late consolation for Albert Hopoate.

And with Leigh still having five of their last seven games to play at home, they do not look like going away in the race for the top six.

Giants end 12-match losing run with win at York

Since losing to Warrington in successive weeks in April in Super League and the Challenge Cup, the Leopards had won 10 out of 12 games, including victory over the Wire at Magic Weekend three weeks ago and they were out of the traps strongly.

Lam's pass found Armstrong hitting the line well from full-back as he sold a dummy and found a gap to the tryline.

The scrum-half was then the recipient of fine play, supporting Umyla Hanley after he had broken through the defence to run under the posts.

The Wolves got themselves on the scoreboard thanks to the might of Sipley as three defenders could not keep out the Niue prop at close range.

However, Leigh made it a two-score game again right on half-time as Senior finished off in the left corner after more good work in the line from the half-backs.

The second period saw no quarter given and both sides lost a player to the sin-bin in the early stages. Super League's record try scorer Josh Charnley was penalised for head contact on Toby King, while Warrington scrum-half Leon Hayes joined him for a dangerous tackle on Owen Trout.

And with emotions running high, Ofahengaue profited as sheer brute force saw him force his way over.

Moments later, the contest was settled as Hanley scored a try that legendary father Ellery would have been proud of as a combination of strength, footwork and handling skills took him past a clutch of defenders in a small space.

With their defence relishing the battle, it was a good tune-up for the visit of neighbours Wigan Warriors on Friday (20:00).

Hopoate's try came too late in this one to make any difference for Warrington and they will have to regroup ahead of their trip to Castleford Tigers the following day to regain momentum in the play-off battle.

Leigh Leopards head coach Adrian Lam said:

"I'm happy. Just relieved in a sense, especially second half where we had a few injuries, it could have been really tight - they had the majority of the ball - but we defended really well at times and the way we hung in there as a group was inspirational.

"The second half, we had to play within [ourselves], I saw the boys were gassed and with only two subs, it was going to be a tough 40 minutes but the players were unbelievably good.

"We were really physical. They were fired up at the start of the game but once it settled down, some of our rugby was as good as we've played this season."

Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess told Sky Sports:

"It is one of those games. I thought the scoreline probably didn't reflect the game or how tight the game was.

"In that second half I thought we started with great spirit. We just couldn't get any points."

title: Ipswich sign Japan forward Maeda from Celtic
description: Ipswich Town sign Japan forward Daizen Maeda from Celtic on a contract until summer 2029.
fullText:
Ipswich Town have signed Japan forward Daizen Maeda from Celtic on a three-year contract.

The 28-year-old, who has joined the Premier League side in a reported £10m deal,, external was part of his country's squad at the 2026 World Cup and helped them reach the last 32 before they were knocked out by Brazil.

Maeda scored 79 goals in 212 appearances at Celtic, where he won five league titles, three Scottish Cups and two League cups.

"I have always dreamed of playing in the Premier League and I am very happy I can realise that dream with this club," Maeda told Ipswich's website., external

"I have loved all of the conversations with the club and they have made me feel very welcome.

"My aim will always be to battle hard, score goals, and provide assists for my team - I will always run and give everything that I have."

Ipswich manager Gary O'Neil, who took over at Portman Road in the summer following the departure of Kieran McKenna, believes Maeda will be "a valuable member" of his squad.

Maeda joins the Tractor Boys following their promotion back into the top flight after they finished second in the Championship under McKenna last season.

"He works extremely hard and has impressive physical attributes, while also proving over a number of years playing in Scotland that he has the ability to score goals and create for his team," said O'Neil.

Ipswich have added Maeda to the arrivals of defender Issa Diop, winger Abdul Fatawu, striker Emersonn and goalkeeper Kayne van Oevelen.

In addition, defender Cedric Kipre and forward Chuba Akpom signed on a permanent basis following successful loans last season.

In a social media post, external to the "Celtic family", Maeda said "the last four and a half years at Celtic have been the most special chapter of my career and my life".

He added: "It has been an incredible honour to wear this badge, to play for this amazing club, and to share so many unforgettable moments with my teammates, the staff, and the best supporters in the world.

"Thank you for standing by me through every high and low."

When Maeda joined Celtic as a relatively unknown J-League attacker in 2022, no one could have imagined the kind of success he would go on to have at the club.

Maeda arrived in the early days of the Ange Postecoglou era, making the switch from Yokohoma F Marinos to Glasgow initially on loan in late December 2022 before completing a permanent switch in the following summer.

His pace and energy has helped Celtic on numerous occasions but the 2025-26 campaign is what he will be most fondly remembered for.

After failing to replace Kyogo Furuhashi up front, Celtic relied on Maeda to play through the middle for almost the entirety of last season.

Having initially struggled for form, he turned things around when it mattered most.

Maeda was on a barren run of just one goal in 18 games and Celtic were second in the table, trailing league leaders Hearts.

What followed was transformational. Maeda scored seven goals in five Premiership matches, two of which were game winners.

He scored the unforgettable second goal in the final-day decider at home to Hearts when, with the score level at 1-1, Maeda fired beyond Alexander Schwolow on 87 minutes to send Celtic Park wild.

In his final game for Celtic, Maeda opened the scoring in a comfortable Scottish Cup final win over Dunfermline Athletic.

While many fans will be sad to see him go, they probably feel it is a deserved move for a player that has contributed so much.

"His relentless energy and vital goals were an essential part of the team over the past four-and-a-half years, and he was a firm favourite with Celtic fans," said a Celtic statement., external

"As he heads on to pastures new at Ipswich Town, everyone at Celtic thanks Daizen for his contribution to the club over the past few years and we wish him all the best for the future."

title: 1.6 million cartons of eggs are recalled over potential salmonella contamination
description: The recall affects white-shell and cage-free eggs sold under multiple grocery brands in six states. No illnesses have been reported.
fullText:
Midwest Poultry Services is recalling nearly 1.6 million cartons of eggs over concerns that they could be contaminated with salmonella, the Food and Drug Administration said Wednesday.

The recall covers white-shell and brown cage-free shell eggs produced at the company's Texas farms and distributed to retailers in six states.

Salmonella Enteritidis can cause serious and sometimes fatal infections in vulnerable populations such as young children or older adults. Symptoms in otherwise healthy people can include fever, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting.

The recalled eggs from Texas farms were produced and distributed to customers across six states between June 6 and July 3, according to the FDA's recall notice. Their sell-by or best-by dates are between July 20 and Aug. 17, and they were sold under multiple brand names, including Kroger, Simple Truth, Brookshire's, Country Morning and Sunups.

Here's where the recalled eggs were sold:

Arkansas: Brookshire Grocery storesLouisiana: Kroger, Brookshire Grocery storesMississippi: Brookshire Grocery storesNew Mexico: Brookshire Grocery storesOklahoma: Brookshire Grocery storesTexas: Kroger, Brookshire Grocery stores

The eggs were also sold at other smaller retail outlets, according to the FDA, which said that no other products for the poultry firm are part of the latest recall.

No illnesses have been reported related to the eggs, according to Midwest Poultry Services.

The firm identified the issue through what it described as "proactive environmental monitoring practices and root cause analysis" on its two Texas farms. It has since paused the distribution of any fresh eggs produced at the farms.

Consumers should not eat the recalled eggs and should return them to the place of purchase for a full refund. A complete list of affected products is available in the FDA's recall notice.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect that the FDA said nearly 1.6 million dozen eggs are being recalled.

title: Defeated progressive ‘Squad’ lawmaker in hot seat for non-profit’s missing paper trail
description: Missouri's attorney general is investigating whether Cori Bush personally benefited from tornado relief fundraising tied to Politivist Power Inc.
fullText:
Months before losing re-election, former Rep. Cori Bush, D-Mo., touted the work of her non-profit to donors even though records indicate the organization may have never been registered as a tax-exempt organization.

Bush described Poltivist Power Inc. as "a new 501(c)(4) organization uniting grassroots organizing with political strategy to fight oppression," in a fundraising email.

"My team and I are on the ground, and we could use your support. Can we count on you to donate to our tornado fund today so we can continue our relief efforts?" Bush wrote.

Stacey Abrams Hit With Subpoena In Alleged Campaign Finance Violations Saga: 'No One Is Above The Law'

Bush made the same characterization in a second fundraising email sent weeks later.

But Fox News Digital could not identify any IRS record showing Poltivist Power had obtained or claimed tax-exempt status. While not proof of wrongdoing, the lack of a paper trail for Bush's organization raises questions about whether the former "Squad" member misled donors during her time in office.

Without reporting, it's unclear how much the group fundraised.

Bush, who first arrived to Congress in 2021, was known for her progressive stances that grouped her with fellow Democrats like Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich.

Among them, Bush began taking a critical view of the U.S. relationship with Israel amid its protracted war with Hamas in Gaza. Her criticisms became a centerpiece topic in her 2024 primary against Democratic challenger Wesley Bell — a race she lost.

Now out of office, Bush has remained involved in progressive politics in her local scene.

When approached about Poltivist Power Inc., Bush did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital on whether Poltivist Power had received donations, on why it hadn't yet reported a 990 and about the nature of its activities.

The organization's domain, Poltivistpower.com, was first purchased on April 1, 2025, records show. Bush announced the creation of the group shortly after a tornado struck the St. Louis area, killing at least four people and causing widespread damage.

'Squad' Dem Dismisses Fraud Probe Speculation After $29M Net-worth Drop

"The Politivist team is on the ground, providing supplies, checking on families, and showing up for those who've been left behind," Bush said.

Since then, in addition to not having a filing recorded with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the group seem to have wrongly filed paperwork with Delaware's Department of State and with ActBlue Civics, a fundraising site for Democratic groups.

In its March 2025 Delaware incorporation filing, Poltivist Power was registered as an "exempt" corporation, a designation Delaware says is reserved for entities that meet the requirements of Section 501 of the Internal Revenue Code.

In both cases, the application requires tax-exempt status with the IRS. The organization is still listed on ActBlue Civics.

Notably, Bush's fundraising emails, in which she highlighted the organization, also included a disclaimer clarifying that "Contributions to Politivist Power are not affiliated with Politivist Action PAC and are not political donations." The note distinguishes the non-profit from a dedicated fundraising group by the same name.

Despite Bush's departure from Congress, enough anomalies about Politivist Power have surfaced to catch the attention of Missouri Attorney General Catherine L. Hanaway earlier this month.

She announced her office would look into whether Bush had personally benefited from her fundraising efforts during the tornado recovery and the work that Politivist allegedly did at the time.

"The investigation started when a local news station reported that people had reported to it that contributions they had made for a tornado relief fund had actually gone to her political activity," Hanaway said in a statement about the investigation.

"We do not have our own evidence of that, but that is what we are investigating," she added.

Bush has not been formally charged with any wrongdoing.

description: A 67-year-old Florida man allegedly rammed a woman's car with his truck and pointed a Ruger at her friend after a Tinder sugar baby date went wrong.
fullText:
A 67-year-old man's search for a "sugar baby" ended with him allegedly pointing a rifle at a 22-year-old after ramming a car into a telephone pole, according to his arrest report.

David Allen O'Brien, who lives in The Villages, a sprawling retirement community in central Florida, was arrested Tuesday on charges of aggravated assault after allegedly chasing down a 21-year-old woman he had paid in a "sugar baby" arrangement and ramming her car with his truck, according to the arrest report.

The arrest report details how O'Brien met the woman on the dating app Tinder and told her he was "looking for a sugar baby," a romantic arrangement that typically involves an older man spending lavishly on a younger woman.

Florida Man Who Allegedly Lured Women With Dating App Could Have More Victims: Authorities

The pair agreed to meet July 21, and O'Brien told the woman he would give her $1,000 "each visit ... dinner and I love to shop for you," according to the affidavit.

The woman showed up to dinner with three friends waiting in the car, according to the affidavit.

When she arrived, O'Brien gave the woman $200 and took her shopping for lingerie. They then went to dinner, where he gave her another $600. Afterward, they went back to his home where she "began to feel uncomfortable and contacted her friends to come pick her up," the arrest report reads.

Florida Man Who Allegedly Lured Women With Dating App Could Have More Victims: Authorities

"The defendant stated he began to massage [the woman's] feet and she was on her phone the entire time. The defendant advised [the woman] went to the bathroom and when she came out she stated she was going to call an Uber to pick her up," the report states.

O'Brien then told the woman she "should give the money back because that was not the agreement," the report adds. She got into her friends' car, at which point O'Brien allegedly began chasing them in his Ford F-150 truck.

When the four friends reached a traffic circle, O'Brien rammed their car with his truck, forcing it to crash into a telephone pole, according to the affidavit. Three of them fled, but when the fourth, a 22-year-old male, attempted to leave, he was met by O'Brien allegedly pointing a gun in his face.

Florida Man Who Allegedly Lured Women With Dating App Could Have More Victims: Authorities

"The defendant pointed his 22 semi-automatic Ruger at him and told him to get on the ground or he would kill him," the arrest report read.

The man "was on the ground face down and noticed that the defendant was distracted so he was able to move to safety."

When police arrived, they found O'Brien at his truck with his weapon in possession, according to the arrest report.

O'Brien claimed the car he was chasing had its tail lights blacked out, a sign, to him, that meant he had been "scammed," according to the arrest report.

O'Brien was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without the intent to kill and aggravated battery. He was transferred to Sumter County Jail "without incident," according to the arrest report.

His arraignment is scheduled for Aug. 14, according to Sumter County records.

title: Daughter Charlotte inspires Firth to bronze medal
description: Team Northern Ireland swimmer Bethany Firth reflects on winning bronze in the S14 200m freestyle, an event she admits she has struggled with since coming back to the sport after giving birth.
fullText:
Gold was the colour four years ago in Birmingham, but Bethany Firth was forced to settle for bronze in Glasgow this time round.

She finished third in the women's S14 200m freestyle in a time of 2:07.63 as her Team GB compatriots English duo Georgia Sheffield and Poppy Maskill pipped her on the podium.

Still, a medal is a medal and there was little time for disappointment, if Firth felt any, to fester as she was swiftly reunited with her young daughter Charlotte after collecting the medal.

The bronze is a significant one in a personal sense as it is the 30-year-old's first major medal since giving birth to Charlotte almost two years ago in August 2024.

Given Charlotte was in attendance in Glasgow, there is no doubt therefore that it will rank as the most sentimental of her impressive haul that includes six Paralympic golds.

Charlotte certainly looked to be appreciating a new medal to fidget with as she clung tightly to it while Bethany was interviewed.

What is more impressive is that Firth pushed through with her daughter at the forefront of her mind and made it on the podium after admitting the freestyle is an event she has struggled to find her rhythm in since making her comeback after giving birth.

"It was a real mental battle going into that and those girls are so good, so just to stand up there, give it my all and get a medal [is great]," she told BBC Sport NI.

"This is an event that hasn't come back as quickly as the others after having Charlotte so to put it together and come away with a medal, I'm really chuffed."

Firth wins NI's first medal with bronze in S14 200m

Charlotte may only be approaching her second birthday and learning how to speak, but she has inspired her mum at these Games more than she will ever know.

Firth was going through the motions right up until being summoned to the call room to go out and race in the final, but seeing her daughter in the crowd spurred her on to push aside the doubts and do what she does best - compete.

She started well at the Tollcross Swimming Centre before the "talented" Sheffield surged into gold and Maskill edged her out for second, but Firth's smile on the podium showed that choosing to see the race through was a fruitful decision.

"I think she made me stronger, I really struggled and thought 'is it worth going into this call room, coming and not getting what I want?' But I kept thinking what would I say to Charlotte and she was there at the end of the lane cheering me on," Firth added.

"I'm so glad I went out there and did it when it was hard."

The 30-year-old has already emphatically defied those who "annoyed" her by assuming she would retire after having a baby by coming back strongly.

She broke her own world record in her stronger event the S14 100m backstroke at the Dutch National Championships in Eindhoven earlier this month.

The LA Olympics in two years time is a realistic target based on recent performances, but raising her daughter has now taken priority over swimming so it's too early to look ahead to 2028 as she continues to navigate day by day balancing the two.

"I'm just taking every year as it comes, I don't know what God has in store for me, we'll just keep taking it year by year and try really hard."

title: Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight
description: The Mediterranean diet was a blueprint for healthy living, yet Italian children are among the most overweight in Europe according to WHO.
fullText:
Daily life is not easy for Salvatore. At 17, he weighs 170kg (26st 10lb) and struggles to walk.

He can't tie his own shoelaces and his Vespa scooter strains to bear his weight - in one week, its wheels broke seven times.

"He eats constantly," says his mother Anna.

Salvatore is among a growing number of Italian children and teenagers living with obesity. The problem is particularly acute in the south: in parts of the Campania region, more than 40% of eight and nine-year-olds are overweight. The town of Ponticelli, on the outskirts of Naples, has earned the unenviable reputation as one of the world's child obesity capitals.

It is a striking development in a country long regarded as the spiritual home of the Mediterranean diet. Yet today, Italian children are among the most overweight in Europe, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Salvatore is waiting for life-changing surgery at the Betania Hospital in Ponticelli, where Dr Sonja Chiappetta has spent 15 years treating patients with severe obesity.

Until recently, she says, most of her patients were in their fifties. "Now I see those same patients when they're teenagers, as young as 16. They are getting younger, and it's frightening."

The surgery she carries out removes up to 90% of the stomach - meaning people are unable to eat large quantities of food. Demand has risen sharply in this part of Italy.

But Salvatore has been told he cannot get the operation. His weight is so excessive it makes the surgery too dangerous.

Instead, Dr Chiappetta has prescribed him a GLP-1 weight-loss injection to reduce his appetite and help him lose enough weight for the operation.

For decades, Italy was held up as a model of healthy eating.

The Mediterranean diet - rich in vegetables, legumes, olive oil, whole grains and fish - became famous after US physiologist Ancel Keys and his wife, biochemist Margaret Keys, studied communities in southern Italy in the 1950s and linked their habits to remarkably low rates of heart disease.

Their research transformed a regional way of eating into one of the world's best-known diets; a blueprint for healthy living.

But the Italy that inspired those studies no longer exists.

"The traditional Mediterranean diet has been lost," says Doctor Valter Longo, director of the Longevity Institute at the University of Southern California. "Only 10% of Italians really follow it."

Dr Longo sums up the modern Italian diet with what he calls the "five Ps": pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein and pane - the Italian word for bread.

The transformation is visible everywhere: from supermarket shelves stocked with ultra-processed foods to pizzerias selling slices piled high with chips, sausages and fried snacks.

Doctor Roberto Berni Canani, a paediatrician and obesity specialist at the Federico II University in Naples, sees the consequences every day.

"I've treated children who are just two or three years old and already weigh 25kg," he says.

He says most parents don't recognise their children are overweight. "They come to see me because of other problems - a cough, stomach pain, diarrhoea. They don't realise their child's weight is what's causing it."

Ten-year-old Francesca has a persistent cough and struggles to swallow. Doctors suspect an inflammatory condition of the oesophagus.

She weighs 60kg (9st 6lb) - but that's not why her parents have sought medical help.

Francesca says she eats bread with Nutella for breakfast, a chocolate-filled sponge cake as a snack, pasta with lentils for lunch and usually chicken for dinner.

"But she doesn't eat vegetables," her mother, Carmen, interjects. "I put them in front of her, but she won't touch them."

Francesca's parents insist she is active. She does artistic gymnastics and Latin dance, and doesn't get tired. They have never considered her weight as a problem.

Dr Berni Canani reaches a different conclusion.

The problem, he explains, is the overall pattern rather than any single meal. Small, calorie-dense foods consumed throughout the day, sugary drinks, too few fruit and vegetables and little understanding of how these habits accumulate over time.

"This is a very good mother," he says. "A very good father. They simply don't recognise the importance of diet quality and body weight."

And in Italy, encouraging children to be more active can be surprisingly difficult.

Many schools are housed in beautiful old palazzi - they were never designed with modern physical education in mind.

The Ugo Foscolo primary school is no exception. Its gym has barely enough space for a class of children to move around.

"I have one pupil I'm particularly concerned about," says Francesca Pecce, who teaches at the school. "He's 10 years old and weighs around 60 kilograms."

She has tried raising the issue with his mother.

"But she is not worried," Pecce says. "In Neapolitan culture, if a child is a little chubby with rosy cheeks, people often think they're healthy."

Schools, she believes, can help change that, especially if children "take home" lessons about healthy eating.

"Sometimes it's easier to educate the parents through their children than the other way round."

At a secondary school in Naples, students file into a classroom for a nutrition workshop run by the Valter Longo Foundation.

The programme is part of a regional initiative to tackle childhood obesity. Over the coming months, more than 17,000 students across 25 schools will take part. Families will receive support to help change eating habits at home.

But not all of the students are convinced.

Eighteen-year-old Ciro doubts that information alone will change behaviour.

"My classmates already know what's healthy," he says. "They just don't care."

Carmen, 19, is more optimistic.

"I thought it was actually really helpful because teenagers today are really big into junk food, and don't exercise as much."

She says the problem is that temptation is everywhere. Even foods traditionally associated with Italy have changed.

"When we go out for pizza, people don't just order a Margherita. They put chips, sausages and fried food on top."

Add to that the centuries-old cliches of Italian mothers and grandmothers showing their love through food, and it's a perfect storm.

Obesity is an "escalating global epidemic", says the WHO. More than one billion people worldwide are now obese, and childhood obesity has quadrupled since 1990.

In 2025, Italy became the first country to pass a national law recognising obesity as a chronic, progressive and relapsing disease.

Rather than treating obesity simply as the result of poor choices, the country's new law recognises it as a chronic disease influenced by biology, environment and social circumstances.

The Campania region has become a testing ground for putting that philosophy into practice, implementing a series of ambitious interventions - including a controversial trial of a "fast-mimicking diet".

Researchers are recruiting 300 overweight adolescents who will spend five days every three months on a controlled diet of 1,100 calories on day one and 770 calories on following four days - so restrictive it resembles a fast.

The goal is to trigger a "metabolic reset".

"Fasting, or controlled deprivation of food, is linked to a longer and healthier lifespan," says Dr Longo, who has spent three decades studying the effects of fasting.

But not all obesity specialists are persuaded that fasting is the right approach for children.

Paediatrician Berni Canani believes the evidence for fasting-mimicking diets in children is still too limited to be recommended in Italy's clinical guidelines.

He also worries restrictive diets could carry psychological risks for adolescents, whose relationship with food is still developing.

"I fear that imposing food restrictions on teenagers could increase the risk of eating disorders, anorexia and body dysmorphia," he says.

Meanwhile, Salvatore hopes to have surgery in the summer, so that, for the first time in years, he can wear a swimming costume without feeling self-conscious.

But he is not alone. Across Italy, a generation of children is growing up increasingly removed from the Mediterranean diet that once made the country famous.

title: Norris on pole as Hamilton and Antonelli penalised
description: McLaren's Lando Norris takes his first grand prix pole position of 2026 in Hungary, as Lewis Hamilton and Kimi Antonelli are both given grid penalties.
fullText:
McLaren's Lando Norris took his first grand prix pole position of the season in Hungary - but Lewis Hamilton was denied the chance to make it an all-British front row by a penalty for impeding.

A three-place penalty for blocking Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri has dropped Hamilton to fifth on the grid, and may have erased his chances of a ninth victory on a track he has almost made his own in his 20-year career.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who originally qualified fourth, was also given a three-place grid penalty for not slowing sufficiently under single yellow flags, following a spin for Red Bull's Max Verstappen at the final corner.

The penalties mean Ferrari's Charles Leclerc will start second, Piastri third, Verstappen fourth and Hamilton fifth, with Mercedes' George Russell sixth, a place ahead of team-mate Antonelli.

Hamilton had been fastest on the first runs, by just over 0.1secs from Norris, but neither the seven-time champion nor Leclerc could improve on their final attempts.

Verstappen's error affected Antonelli and Russell, who were forced to slow, although in the Italian's case the stewards decided it was not by enough.

Verstappen had got going again before Norris came around as the last driver on track to clinch pole in the upgraded McLaren by just 0.012 seconds.

Norris cautious despite pole as it 'falls apart' for Hamilton

Malaysia set to host F1 race in October

Norris said: "Very happy to be back on top, especially at a track where you certainly want to be on pole.

"I had confidence the whole of today. My laps in Q3 were not the best, even the one at the end, so pleasantly surprised to be on top."

Hamilton was a second slower on his second run than on his first and was unhappy he had been sent out for it first.

"I had a clean out-lap, and when I started my lap, already into Turn One I had a snap and I was already 0.15secs down," Hamilton said. "It just cascaded from there.

"So, the last lap was the worst lap of all, and all the other laps were really good. We clearly had the car to be on pole today, and I just didn't deliver. So that's tough to swallow."

On the impeding scenario, Hamilton said he had not been warned of Piastri's approach by the team: "I was told literally when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming.

"I was the first out, so I thought everyone had finished their lap. Charles, I think, was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn't intentional."

Verstappen railed about the unpredictable handling of the Red Bull over the radio after his spin. His team-mate Isack Hadjar starts eighth, ahead of Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.

Fernando Alonso made a major breakthrough for Aston Martin on the weekend they debuted their virtually new car by breaking out of the first session for the first time this season.

Alonso will start 16th, 2.8secs off pole - but that was two seconds faster in relative pace than they had managed for some time.

The veteran Spaniard, who is 45 next week, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I feel relieved a little bit, feeling that the team understood the weaknesses of the car and this is the first step in the right direction.

"We brought a few updates to this car early in the season, and it didn't work much. And we come from two years of disappointments of upgrades. So definitely there is a change in optimism in the factory and I feel optimistic."

Alonso faces a decision this summer as to whether to continue his career after this season. He said that while he had no doubts managing technical partner Adrian Newey would lead the team to success in the future, he was not sure whether it would happen soon enough for him.

"No-one should doubt Adrian Newey or the potential we have in Silverstone. It is a matter of time before we have the best chassis and it is a matter of time before Honda have the best engine in F1. It is a question of when."

All the drivers were battling with a Hungaroring track surface that was breaking up, especially in the final two corners, where Norris said it was especially difficult to judge the grip level.

Even before the incident with Verstappen, Russell was afflicted on his final run by a water leak, which was spraying water on to his rear tyres.

Mercedes asked him to pull over immediately after crossing the line, and he parked at Turn One, in an attempt to avoid damaging the engine.

Speaking before his penalty, Antonelli said: "I think we were just slightly out of the window with tyres, then in Q3 we did a good step and the car just felt finally a bit more alive. For sure it was a shame with the yellow flags, but it happens. P3 was on the table today but still not good enough for pole."

title: Gymnast Langton cleared of serious injury after shocking fall
description: English gymnast Gabriel Langton is cleared of serious injury after a sickening fall at the Commonwealth Games on Friday.
fullText:
English gymnast Gabriel Langton has been cleared of serious injury after a sickening fall at the Commonwealth Games on Friday.

Langton fell head first from three metres to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal metal bar during the opening day of competition and was taken to hospital.

Team England said Langton underwent "multiple scans" on Saturday with "very positive results".

The 19-year-old, who has not qualified for any remaining events at the Games, will be discharged from hospital on Saturday evening.

"He is in good spirits and hugely grateful for the many messages of support and the excellent care provided by the medical teams," a statement said.

"He is looking forward to being reunited with the team to celebrate his silver medal."

Commonwealth Games: Ramsay-Peaty in swimming finals, England in women's gymnastics team final - radio & text

There was a lengthy halt to proceedings after Langton's fall before he was taken away on a stretcher.

When the competition resumed, his team-mates secured a silver medal behind Canada, though Langton is yet to receive his.

After the incident, team-mate Luke Whitehouse said: "When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time."

Canada's Felix Dolci said: "It's terrible but it goes to show that gymnastics is a very, very difficult and complicated sport. It's dangerous you know sometimes.

"All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team."

Langton was a late call-up to Team England in the place of the injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock.

title: Ukraine is still fortifying its border with Belarus years after Russia invaded from there
description: ALONG THE UKRAINE-BELARUS BORDER (AP) — More than four years after Russia launched its assault on Kyiv from Belarus, Ukraine is still fortifying the border it shares with Moscow's ally.  The Associate...
fullText:
ALONG THE UKRAINE-BELARUS BORDER (AP) — More than four years after Russia launched its assault on Kyiv from Belarus, Ukraine is still fortifying the border it shares with Moscow's ally. What was once a busy crossing between the two countries is now a quiet, mine-laden stretch of land closed off to civilians.

Roads near the 1,084-kilometer-long (673-mile-long) border are covered for long distances by anti-drone netting. The surrounding landscape is dominated by rows of razor wire and concrete anti-tank barriers known as "dragon's teeth."

The Associated Press visited parts of the border in northern Ukraine earlier this month, following a rise in tensions between the two countries; Ukraine demanded that Belarus shut down communications relay stations Russia had installed to boost the range of its drones attacking Ukrainian cities.

Belarus obliged, according to Ukraine, and rhetoric between the two governments has eased since then. While Ukrainian officials say they see no signs of a Russian troop buildup in Belarus, they are determined to strengthen their border against any possible threat.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has repeatedly said he has no plans for his troops to enter the war unless his country is attacked. Still, people living near the border say the possibility of Belarus becoming more involved in Russia's war remains a source of anxiety.

For many residents, the extensive defenses are both a reminder of the early days of the war and a source of reassurance that Ukraine is preparing for any future scenarios.

Ukrainian border guards patrol the area around the clock using armored vehicles, drones and other surveillance systems. Ukrainian officials say the addition of more defenses will remain a priority well into the future because Belarus is Russia's closest military ally.

title: Drone threat in Russia's Yekaterinburg disrupts Wildberries operations and athletics championships
description: YEKATERINBURG, Russia July 25 (Reuters) - A drone threat prompted leading Russian online retailer Wildberries to evacuate its logistics hub on Saturday in the city of Yekaterinburg, where the national
fullText:
YEKATERINBURG, Russia July 25 (Reuters) - A drone threat prompted leading Russian online retailer Wildberries to evacuate its logistics hub on Saturday in the city of Yekaterinburg, where ‌the national athletics championships were also briefly suspended.

Ukraine has struck Wildberries' warehouses in a string ‌of attacks over the past week, broadening its long-range drone strategy to target a company central to Russia's consumer ​economy.

Wildberries said it had temporarily halted operations at the Yekaterinburg facility for security reasons, but that the site had not been damaged. Around four hours later, it said operations had resumed.

Earlier on Saturday, local authorities declared a drone alert over the wider Sverdlovsk region and said one attack had been repelled ‌over Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city. Falling ⁠drone debris set fire to a parking lot, Governor Denis Pasler wrote on the Telegram app.

"Economic and infrastructure facilities were not damaged," he said, cautioning ⁠residents to remain vigilant as the drone threat persisted.

The alert also delayed the penultimate day of competition at the Russian Athletics Championships, which the city was hosting.

Athletes and spectators had to leave the open stadium ​and ​take shelter, according to a Reuters witness.

"This has never ​happened to me at competitions, but in ‌everyday life it has. Sometimes, even during training, we'll have drone alerts and sirens going off. So, it's a normal atmosphere, so to speak," said runner Anastasia Fedonina from the southwestern Volgograd region.

Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian infrastructure this year in a bid to undermine its war effort and pressure the Kremlin to make peace. It says it has targeted Wildberries ‌on the grounds that it handles military supplies, which ​the Kremlin has denied.

Since launching its full-scale invasion of ​Ukraine in 2022, Russia has repeatedly targeted ​Ukrainian logistics infrastructure, as well as its energy system and power grid.

On Saturday, ‌local authorities in Russia's southern Krasnodar region ​said open flames had ​been extinguished at a warehouse hit by drones on Wednesday. They did not name the facility, but a Wildberries warehouse in Krasnodar was attacked that day.

Together with smaller rivals, Wildberries ​and top competitor Ozon sell ‌goods and services worth the equivalent of 8.5% of Russia's gross domestic product and ​employ 4 million people, or more than 5% of the country's workforce.

title: 'Mind-blowing' El Niño stuns scientists. Why are they so concerned?
description: A Pacific El Niño is setting daily warm water records. Scientists say the world is in uncharted waters, and they aren't sure what will happen next.
fullText:
The world's most influential climate pattern is baring its teeth in the Pacific.

The strengthening El Niño – a natural warming of seawater that influences weather around the planet – is setting daily warm water records.

It's not only "very likely to be the strongest event since reliable records began – it may end up the strongest by a truly mind-blowing margin," Zeke Hausfather, a research scientist at Berkeley Earth, wrote in a post for The Climate Brink, a Substack blog, earlier in July.

It remains to be seen what this will mean for the world's weather over the next 12 to 18 months, but climate scientists say El Niño's effects on global temperatures will increase the chances that 2026 could be the warmest year on record, and make it likely that 2027 will be the warmest.

Meanwhile, world leaders have expressed concern about the prospect of droughts, heavy rainfall events and heat waves. (It's worth noting, however, that not all El Niño effects are sinister. The climate pattern is widely expected to tame the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane season.)

Economy: 'Super El Niño' will have an alarming financial impact, experts fear

El Niño impacts are already being felt in the U.S., suppressing Atlantic hurricane activity and bringing unusual heat and humidity to parts of California, one of the states most vulnerable to El Niño's impacts.

Sea surface temperatures already have crossed the threshold that typically marks a very strong event, Hausfather and Robert Rohde, his colleague at Berkeley Earth, wrote in a monthly climate briefing on July 23.

The warming trajectory of sea surface temperatures in the El Niño region along the equator has been "remarkable," developing faster than the 1997-98 El Niño, Hausfather wrote in the earlier post.

NOAA data shows water temperatures in the region have never run this hot in July in the modern record.

While El Niño is a naturally occurring pattern, concerns are growing about its amplified impacts when combined with the climate change-fueled warmer-than-normal temperatures around the globe.

The world is looking at "an unprecedented combination" between the strong El Niño and the elevated warmth from climate change, said Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources. That will influence what El Niño actually means on the ground in the U.S. and across the world, Swain said.

Previous El Niño events temporarily raised global temperatures about 0.54 degrees Fahrenheit, he said. Now the globe will have the effects of long-term human-caused warming with additional warming on top of that.

"A potentially record-breaking El Niño on top of record-breaking global temperatures to begin with is a pretty big deal," he said.

"The odds of either this year or next year, or both, setting a new record warm average global temperature are high," Swain said. "If we don't get there this year, we almost certainly will next year."

Sea surface temperatures in the El Niño region of the Pacific are up to 6 degrees warmer than normal for the date, a phenomenon that is several times more likely because of climate change, according to Climate Central, a nonprofit climate science and communications organization.

"What is most striking is how strong this event is forecast to become," wrote Hausfather and Rohde in their briefing. The vast majority of computer models predict an El Niño that exceeds the 2015-2016 record event, even taking into account the background ocean warming, the pair concluded. It's "more likely than not to be the strongest El Niño ever observed."

A "very strong" El Niño can influence weather worldwide.

"El Niño will give an extra boost to global temperatures," stated Alvaro Silva, a World Meteorological Organization scientist. "We know that during El Niño years, the global temperatures normally reach record levels."

In the U.S., a strong El Niño means "a pretty robust increase in the jet stream," Swain said. "That can result in more intense and more frequent winter storms in California, the interior southwest and the southern tier of states."

"Some of California's wettest winters have occurred during some of the strongest El Niños," he said.

El Niño can heighten hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific and suppress hurricane activity in the Atlantic.

Because of its influence on hydrologic cycles, El Niño can bring catastrophic floods to some regions but severe drought and wildfires to others. It can also disrupt fisheries and food production and bring about trillions of dollars in economic losses.

"The current forecasts imply this could be the costliest El Niño on record," Justin Mankin, a Dartmouth geography associate professor who studies El Niño's economic impacts, recently told USA TODAY by email.

Specifically, there are likely to be drier-than-average conditions in Central America and the Caribbean, along with North and South America, the United Nations said. Drier weather patterns are also forecast in parts of Indonesia and Southeast Asia during the monsoon season, but wetter conditions are anticipated during the rainy season from September to December in East Africa.

Even though the signals and models point to a strong El Niño, that doesn't mean it will definitely be the strongest on record when it's expected to peak later this year, said climate scientist Michael Mann, director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability & the Media at the University of Pennsylvania.

"It's clear we are headed towards an historically strong event," Mann said, but "there's still a variety of scenarios we could see."

El Niño is intrinsically a chaotic event in a climate system that doesn't always respond in simple, proportional ways, Mann explained. Its greatest impacts come from its connections to the larger atmosphere, such as the trade winds and upper atmospheric winds, but those teleconnections can be hard to predict.

Small differences in conditions such as ocean temperatures or the trade winds can alter what happens later. For example, El Niño's ultimate impacts depend on factors such as where the maximum heating takes place in the equatorial Pacific in the fall and early winter.

Part of the uncertainty rests with the fact that the models are in "uncharted waters," Hausfather wrote. The models have "never been verified in this territory."

It's unusual to see this kind of agreement among the strongest predictive models, but what that will mean remains to be seen, Swain said. "Every event has a different flavor and this will undoubtedly have a different flavor than we've ever seen before."

Dinah Voyles Pulver and Doyle Rice are national correspondents with USA TODAY who have decades of experience writing about weather and climate. Reach them at dpulver@usatoday.com and drice@usatoday.com.
