title: Talarico is trying to win back Hispanics along the Texas border who swung toward the GOP
description: The black campaign bus with “Talarico for Texas” across its side came to a steaming stop at Memo’s Restaurant along the U.S.-Mexico border.  “A lot of people, for some reason, especially the Hispanics...
fullText:
EAGLE PASS, Texas (AP) — The black campaign bus with "Talarico for Texas" across its side came to a steaming stop at Memo's Restaurant along the U.S.-Mexico border. Bibi Valdez's eyes lit up. She marched in heels over to the bus, phone camera trained on its door, chatting about the locals whose political leanings shifted two years ago.

"A lot of people, for some reason, especially the Hispanics, changed to Republican," she said as security guards created space for James Talarico, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate. "I just don't see what the logic was."

Talarico is on a quest to become the first Democrat to win a statewide election in Texas since 1994. Memo's Restaurant was one stop on a winding trip along the border this month, where he was searching for support from the predominantly Hispanic counties that became national political curiosities after the 2024 election.

Once consistently Democratic, most had voted for Republican President Donald Trump, some by a lot, as Hispanic voters shifted to the right nationally. Along this stretch of border, residents and elected leaders alike tend to point to two reasons: the rise in both border crossings and everyday prices. One dropped dramatically since 2024, and it wasn't the cost of eggs.

While Trump has tamped down on illegal border crossings — once Democrats' Achilles' heel — the cost of living is still high, giving Talarico a topic he's been hitting on repeat as he campaigns against Republican Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general.

Whether Talarico's message can sway Hispanic voters who moved to the GOP to return to the Democratic Party will help decide the Senate race, and could determine whether Democrats can win control of the Senate.

So Talarico, a former middle school teacher and state lawmaker, was taking time to shake hands and pose for photos with people outside Memo's Restaurant, which was at capacity with people wanting to see him. Valdez, waiting her turn, pondered aloud why those she knew had voted Republican.

"They thought a better economy, but obviously it didn't," she said, before beaming for a photo with the candidate.

Inside Memo's Restaurant, the crowd was revved up, shoulder to shoulder, below beating fans, as Talarico opened his speech.

"So many politicians show up at the border to demonize and weaponize," Talarico said. "We are doing the opposite. We are showing the beauty of our border communities."

It was one of the few times Talarico referenced the border during his stop, turning instead to an economy he says is rigged to help "mega donors" and criticizing Paxton as a "puppet politician" for the wealthy.

"We can't get ahead no matter how hard we work, no matter how much we save, because the system is rigged against us," he said.

Talarico is not the first Democratic Senate candidate in recent years to draw crowds and give the party hope of winning in the reliably Republican state. Beto O'Rourke went on a similar mission in 2018 and failed.

Republicans remain confident about Texas, but Democrats see some reason for optimism.

While Trump gained with Hispanic voters in 2024, opinions of the president have fallen among Hispanics overall since he took office, according to AP-NORC polling. Only 29% of Hispanic adults nationally approved of his performance as president in a June AP-NORC poll, an apparent drop from 41% at the start of his second term.

In communities along the Rio Grande, which defines the U.S.-Mexico border in Texas, the ebb and flow of migrants isn't an abstract political issue. People here still recall — often with empathy — hundreds huddled in reflective emergency blankets under a bridge, and the hit to local businesses and town coffers.

Little aid, many said, came from President Joe Biden's administration.

"It was a nightmare because of him. Now, you don't see no immigrants," said Hector Flores, 72, sitting with his two friends at a McDonald's in Maverick County, about an hour's drive south of Memo's Restaurant.

Maverick County had one of the sharpest swings toward Trump than any county in the country in 2024, from backing Biden by 10 percentage points in 2020 to supporting Trump by 19.

The three men of varying political persuasions weren't following the Senate race particularly closely. But the issues on their minds were the same ones Talarico and Paxton have been talking about, from high costs to ICE and social issues.

Under past presidents, costs were OK, said Eduardo "Lalo" Riojas, 73, who sat next to Flores. Now, "You go down to HEB to buy merchandise, groceries," he said, trailing off without the right English word.

"Yeah," said Riojas, who supports Talarico. "Mr. Trump is crazy."

For Flores, who works with orphanages across the border in Mexico, those high prices aren't making him question his Republican vote. Nor is he politically moved by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's sometimes lethal operations in the interior, which have ruffled some Trump supporters, both Hispanic and otherwise.

Mike Garcia, 76, who sat across from the two and said he voted for Trump three times in a row, was more wary.

"The ones they're killing, some of them, been here in the United States for years and years and got children," Garcia said.

He said Paxton, who has been impeached, then acquitted, and faced allegations of corruption and extramarital affairs, has a "horrible reputation." But he also is bothered by comments Talarico has made about God's gender, a statement Paxton has used to attack his opponent as he appeals to Texas voters' conservative values.

Garcia still didn't know which candidate he'll support come November.

Paxton has leaned more on immigration enforcement as an issue, including during his own border stop in the Rio Grande Valley.

Speaking in a circle of supporters in McAllen, Paxton first plugged the lawsuits he filed against the Biden administration over immigration enforcement, and his endorsement from the National Border Patrol Council.

He then returned to some of his core attacks on Talarico, including repeating the Democrat's statements that "God is nonbinary," which Talarico — a seminary student — said on the Texas House floor several years ago, citing Scripture.

His campaign's director of Hispanic outreach said Paxton has delivered what Hispanics want, including taking on criminals and companies that gouge consumers, and attacked Talarico as "wimpy."

"Hispanics know Ken Paxton is a strong man who shares our values, and we see in James Talarico a wimpy liberal," Alex Alarcon said. "No one looks at him and thinks, now there's a guy who'll protect us from the cartels."

Talarico didn't avoid talk about immigration enforcement completely during his border tour.

At a news conference, he stood in Sanderson, Texas, alongside local sheriffs to pledge investment in surveillance tech to catch illegal crossings and to hire more border patrol agents and immigration judges.

Later, after a town hall where voters aired their frustrations over affording rent, property taxes and healthcare, Talarico spoke with The Associated Press about what's been happening here.

"The Biden administration failed border communities like this, and so people were feeling disillusioned. They were open to an alternative and Republicans came down here with some big promises," he said.

Now, "they're seeing a lot of those promises weren't kept."

title: Bloodied Kelly battles past Agyarko to retain title
description: Briton Josh Kelly is forced to dig deep to retain his IBF light-middleweight world title in a points win against Ireland's Caoimhin Agyarko.
fullText:
Briton Josh Kelly was forced to dig deep to retain his IBF light-middleweight world title, surviving a spirited late comeback from Belfast's Caoimhin Agyarko to win a narrow points decision in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

Kelly looked in complete control until the complexion of the contest changed when he received a deserved sixth-round point deduction for repeated punches to the back of the head.

The 31-year-old was then bloodied by cuts across his face and a gash on his nose as Agyarko grew in confidence and began to land with increasing success.

But Kelly stood firm through the championship rounds to secure victory, with the judges scoring the contest 114-113, 115-112 and 115-112.

"That was a messy and hard fight. I didn't get cuts from punches like this, it comes from heads and elbows. This is what it looks like when you've got tight skin," Kelly said.

"I knew he [Agyarko] was go to be tricky and awkward. [He had] a good game plan. He tried to make it a good boxing match. I had to show a different side to me at the end and that is what a champions does."

Fighting on the undercard of Anthony Joshua's heavyweight comeback against Kristian Prenga, Sunderland's Kelly claimed his 21st professional victory.

Agyarko, 29, had hoped to become Ireland's first black world champion. Instead, despite a brave second-half comeback, he suffered the first defeat of his professional career in his 30th contest.

Also on the card, WBO super-middleweight champion Hamzah Sheeraz laboured to an underwhelming points win over Simon Zachenhuber.

The 27-year-old Briton was far from his best and struggled to find his rhythm but was awarded a majority decision as he extended his record to 24 wins and one defeat.

Agyarko 'didn't do enough' in world title defeat

The tension between the pair had simmered all week, threatening to boil over at Friday's weigh-in after Kelly vowed to "humiliate" his opponent.

Kelly started with a spring in his step, dropping his hands, smiling and chatting to Agyarko as he controlled the opening exchanges.

The challenger was already showing swelling under his right eye by the second round as Kelly began to let his hands go, firing in sharp combinations.

Fresh from winning the IBF title with a points victory over Bakhram Murtazaliev in January, Kelly looked every inch a confident champion. Agyarko had moments with his jab but struggled to match the champion's speed and movement.

Kelly unloaded with a flurry in the fifth, but the point deduction disrupted his rhythm and Agyarko, renowned for finishing strongly, began to find success with left hooks.

A head clash in the ninth round left Kelly with a cut on his nose. "He doesn't want it," Agyarko's corner shouted in the 10th but Kelly responded with sharp uppercuts.

The final two rounds were tense, with Kelly landing the cleaner work before catching Agyarko with a double left hook in the 12th.

Fighting just two months after stopping Alem Begic to win the vacant WBO title, Londoner Sheeraz controlled the early rounds and landed heavy body shots in the second and third.

But German Zachenhuber, 28, who arrived with a 29-1 record built largely against limited opposition, began to frustrate the champion with his southpaw stance.

Sheeraz walked his opponent down but struggled to find the spite and power that had stopped 19 of his previous 24 opponents.

"I will press him," Sheeraz told trainer Andy Lee, but despite winning every round to that point he appeared reluctant to let his right hand go.

A left hook to the body followed by an uppercut hurt Zachenhuber in the ninth, but Sheeraz could not capitalise.

The scorecards were closer than many expected, with one judge scoring the fight a draw. But cards of 114-114, 115-113 and 116-112 handed Sheeraz a majority decision victory.

"I knew it wasn't good but I didn't think it was that bad," Sheeraz said, dismissing suggestions of any injury to his right hand.

After a hard-fought win, Kelly's attention can now turn to the marquee names in their divisions.

While Sebastian Fundora holds the WBA title, Kelly has set his sights on fellow Matchroom fighter Jaron 'Boots' Ennis.

The unbeaten American is a two-weight world champion and the WBA and WBO light-middleweight champion, boasting 32 stoppages in 36 victories.

"I want it next," Kelly said. "People will be smiling looking at that and saying 'what is he talking about' - but that style of fight is a tricky night for anyone.

"I want the big names in the division. I have already took out one big name in Bakhram Murtazaliev. Let me get the other ones."

Sheeraz, meanwhile, remains in contention for a lucrative match-up against Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez.

The Mexican superstar, who has beaten all eight Britons he has faced, must first get past Christian Mbilli in October for the WBC belt before any potential unification showdown can be discussed.

"I'm sure people are chomping at the bit after that performance, so let's make the big ones happen," Sheeraz said.

title: Vozinha to join Chilean club after World Cup heroics
description: Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, who earned plaudits for his feats during the World Cup, is set to join Chilean side Colo Colo.
fullText:
Vozinha, the Cape Verde goalkeeper who earned plaudits for his World Cup performances, is set to join Chilean side Colo Colo.

The 40-year-old headed to the World Cup without a club after his contract with Portuguese second division side Chaves expired, but he became an overnight sensation by starring in a goalless draw against eventual champions Spain.

He has now found a new club, according to Colo Colo president Anibal Mosa.

"Vozinha will be a Colo Colo player," said Mosa.

"In the coming days he will travel to Chile, undergo the usual medical examinations and then be presented here at the Estadio Monumental."

Mosa said Vozinha's World Cup displays showed he deserved the move, acknowledging the signing also carried marketing appeal for Colo Colo.

The club, based in the Chilean capital of Santiago, sit top of Liga de Primera - the country's top division.

Although the transfer has yet to be finalised, the club teased the signing on social media, external with an image showing Vozinha's familiar curly hair.

The experienced keeper become a cult hero and attracted millions of new followers on social media after Cape Verde claimed their first-ever World Cup point against Spain in the group stage.

Cape Verde, the second smallest nation to ever reach the World Cup finals, went close to upsetting Argentina in the last 32 before exiting the competition with a 3-2 extra-time defeat by Lionel Messi and co, who began the tournament as holders and went on to reach another final.

Vozinha has previously played club football in Slovakia, Angola, Moldova, Cyprus and Portugal.

title: How Eala's Wimbledon run made Filipinos fall in love with tennis
description: Formerly the preserve of the rich, tennis is booming in the basketball- and boxing-obsessed country.
fullText:
Chasing her dream of becoming a world tennis champion, teen athlete Maristella Torrecampo and her father took a gruelling 13-hour bus from her sleepy hillside hometown for her latest match in Manila.

The 14-year-old's mum and four siblings could not join to watch her play; her crowdfunded budget was only enough for two round-trip bus tickets and a few days' worth of meals.

Barely rested from the long journey, and with only her father cheering her on, Torrecampo crushed her Omani opponent in straight sets 6-1, 6-1 on that sweltering Tuesday afternoon at the Rizal Stadium, keeping alive her dream of following in the footsteps of Alexandra Eala, the country's newest sports star.

Torrecampo competed in Manila in July as the Philippines was celebrating Eala's historic Wimbledon run - one that Torrecampo and the entire nation followed on streaming and social media.

Eala, 21, went the farthest any Filipina had gone in a Grand Slam event, reaching the fourth round and eliminating defending champion Iga Swiatek of Poland along the way.

Since her breakout semi-final performance at the Miami Open last year, Eala has re-ignited interest in tennis in the Philippines, a country obsessed with the three B's - basketball, boxing and beauty queens.

To young tennis players like Torrecampo, Eala is an inspiration.

"Like Ate Alex, I want to win at Wimbledon, WTA, and various tournaments around the world," Torrecampo said, referring to Eala with the Filipino word for elder sister.

"She inspired me so much. I looked up to her since I was little," said Torrecampo, who has competed in the Philippine National Games, and in tournaments in Cambodia and Sri Lanka.

"I like her attitude off and on court. Off court, she is really humble. There are a lot of kids like me who look up to her."

Eala came home from London to a hero's welcome, with President Ferdinand Marcos hosting a reception in her honour at Malacanang Palace in Manila.

"I'm so grateful that I am able to share my triumphs, most especially my recent run at Wimbledon, with the country," Eala said at the reception.

"As we say, this is our victory. I cannot begin to describe how overjoyed I am to see how my progress has been received by the Filipino people."

Such recognition from her compatriots, Eala added, made her feel "very seen".

Tennis is an elite sport in the Philippines, an archipelago nation of 112 million people.

Decades of American colonial rule bequeathed the nation with a passion for basketball. Every village has a basketball court and Filipinos are more likely to recognise LeBron James than Roger Federer.

Filipinos' love for rags-to-riches underdog stories and big personalities have also made boxing and beauty pageants just as popular. Boxing legend Manny Pacquiao is still the country's most popular athlete.

Tennis has historically been much less popular - until Eala burst onto the scene.

But this has also exposed how difficult it is for everyday Filipinos to take up the sport. Tennis courts are usually found in rich enclaves and equipment is expensive.

Court rentals in Manila cost around 2,000 pesos ($32; £19) per hour, meaning half a day's play costs half the minimum wage. Even for higher income earners, that's equivalent to a month's worth of groceries.

Tennis coach Jovy Barce knows how hard it is to start playing tennis from scratch, especially for the underprivileged.

Barce told the BBC he started as a ball boy picking up balls on the court as a six-year-old in Caloocan city, on the capital's outskirts. He said players would pay him 100 pesos or roughly two dollars, which he would split between himself and his mum for their household's groceries.

Then, when he was eight, Barce picked up a tennis racket from the bin and started practising. Later, one of the players on the court gave him his old racket.

"Up until this day, I couldn't explain how happy I was when I got it. I used it over and over until I became so confident," Barce said. "No one taught me. I never had a professional coach. It was all self-study."

Barce put himself through college on a sports scholarship. He worked at a hotel and as a motorcycle delivery man, but eventually pursued a career in tennis coaching, starting with just 40 tennis balls.

"I started from nothing, but I tried my best to learn everything because I really wanted to become a coach," he said.

"I practised every day. I was always focused. I did not have the chance to compete abroad since I do not have the money or big sponsors. I only competed in Metro Manila and provinces nearby."

Eala, meanwhile, has been criticised for her elite background. She studied tennis at the Rafael Nadal Academy in Spain. Her mother is a former telecommunications executive while her father is a businessman from a prominent family.

Eala was also seen dancing onstage with Bad Bunny during the Puerto Rican star's concert in Sweden.

But she has taken such criticisms in stride, saying critics fail to see her hard work behind the scenes.

Eala's homecoming from Wimbledon showed how big a star she has become.

Big name sponsors mounted fan events, including a meet-and-greet at a shopping mall in Metro Manila's business district of Makati. Many came with their families.

Some, like Federico Perez and his wife Gilia, drove hours from nearby provinces. The couple booked a hotel to get to the event early and secure the best possible view, even though they didn't have tickets.

"We hope to see Alex in person and hopefully she can sign this. Even if this magazine was published a year ago, I still bought it because it has Alex on the cover," Gilia Perez said.

She said her husband never fails to watch Eala's Wimbledon matches, even if they air in the Philippines late at night.

Eleven-year-old Luca Ong, a young tennis fan, came with his parents.

"My goal in the future is to become the next Alex Eala or Rafa Nadal so that I can represent the Philippines in the future," he said.

Eala's hot streak has also energised tennis hobbyists.

At a Manila tennis court, Celso Mugot said his determination to learn the sport had intensified because of Eala's success. The 33-year-old accountant has been training for three months to keep fit and unwind after work.

"I was definitely inspired by Alex Eala. I saw her progress. I watched her when she was still in a low rank until she climbs up," Mugot told the BBC.

Rafael Santos, a 29-year-old information technology professional, also recently took up tennis as a sport. He said booking tennis courts had been difficult since Eala's breakout Miami Open run last year.

"There are only a few courts in Manila while there are a lot of people who wanted to play and train. That's a bit of a let-down," Santos said.

He said tennis shoes and apparel were also either sold out or in short supply, and some stores had jacked up racket prices.

Felino Palafox, a renowned Filipino architect and urban planner, told the BBC that space was a major challenge in building more tennis courts. Metro Manila is home to close to 16 million people and is one of the world's most densely populated urban centres.

Meanwhile, every village in the Philippines has a basketball court that is easily converted into a beauty pageant runway, and boxing gyms run by prizefighters are spread across major cities.

"Ideally, every barangay (village) should have a tennis court, not just basketball courts," Palafox told the BBC.

"We are fighting for (space for) activities."

Eala is now preparing for the US Open in August, seeking to raise the Philippines' status in tennis even higher.

"That's a wrap on Manila. Thank you for welcoming me, my countrymen," she said in an Instagram story.

"Each and every one of your stories has touched me on a profound level. I leave with a refreshed memory of what I carry when I'm out there playing tennis. And wow, is it a privilege to be part of something bigger than myself. Never been prouder to represent home."

The journey continues too for Torrecampo, the 14-year-old from Iriga city. She said she would be working on calming her pre-match nerves as much as improving her swing.

"I hope that aspiring tennis players would get to reach their dreams too, to become professional tennis players, because more kids will get inspired when they see people achieve great things in tennis," she said.

Her father and coach, Delfin Torrecampo, said he would let her daughter enjoy the sport to ease the pressure she usually feels.

"What I always tell her is to focus on the game. Do whatever you can do, but do not pressure yourself. Even if you know you can beat your opponent, do not be complacent," he told the BBC.

"To people who are in the same situation as us, know that poverty is not a hindrance for you and your family's dreams. The people who keep on fighting and persevering are the same people who have the chance to win.

"You may not win today or tomorrow, but your win will come one day as long as you keep on fighting."

title: Norris cautious despite pole as it 'falls apart' for Hamilton
description: Lando Norris has an opportunity to win his first grand prix of the year in Hungary, but Lewis Hamilton says his positivity is being tested after another penalty.
fullText:
Lando Norris took his first grand prix pole position of the year in Hungary but is cautious about whether he can follow it up with his first victory as world champion.

Perhaps the McLaren driver was casting his mind back to Miami in early May, when he was leading towards the end of the first stint of the race, only for his team to make a strategic misstep and allow Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli to sneak in for a win.

"You can't just rely on one good qualifying, so I need a good race tomorrow," Norris said.

"Then we obviously have a nice summer break, but after that we need to try and repeat it several more times.

"We've been working hard. We know we've been on the back foot, but we're making progress and today certainly shows that."

Much of the attention at the Hungarian Grand Prix has been on the massive upgrade made by Aston Martin on their recalcitrant car, which has provided the troubled team with a major step forward and allowed Fernando Alonso to escape the first qualifying session for the first time all season.

That meant McLaren's own upgrade went under the radar somewhat, but it has been effective.

Still, team principal Andrea Stella, while expressing his satisfaction that the upgrades had enabled them to engage in a fight for pole they did not expect, said Norris' pole was an "overachievement".

McLaren's own good execution of qualifying was one factor, he said, in addition to an under-performance from Ferrari, and perhaps even Antonelli and Mercedes.

Ferrari came into Hungary as most people's favourite, including McLaren's, on the basis that their car is the fastest in the corners, but it lacks engine performance, and this is one of the least power-sensitive tracks on the calendar.

Lewis Hamilton was fastest after the first runs in the final part of qualifying but did not improve on his final lap. Shortly after completing it, he blocked Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri and the stewards imposed a three-place grid penalty.

Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur said the team took responsibility for that because they did not warn Hamilton in time.

The seven-time world champion later posted on Instagram:, external "Sometimes you just can't catch a break. Another weekend when I've been feeling great throughout all the sessions, but then it just falls apart."

Referencing penalties he had been given in the previous two races in Britain and Belgium, Hamilton added: "I always do my best to keep positive - sport is always about the highs and lows, but it's also in the margins.

"Every point counts and you have to seize every opportunity. After three penalties in three weekends, it's becoming difficult to hang on to that positivity.

"Still, I won't let the setbacks take away from the progress we've been making as a team. With the pace we have, I'm hopeful we can get something out of the race tomorrow."

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

For all that Ferrari have been quick, Norris and McLaren have also looked in good shape all weekend. And, at least on this circuit, they have vaulted right to the front, into a position that had been familiar for the past two seasons but not so in 2026.

While sat with Ferrari's Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, Norris said: "I knew the pace was certainly there. It has been all weekend. Even though these guys have been insanely fast, I knew I'd been driving very well, I'd been consistent, and I knew the car had potential.

"We also had the upgrades this weekend, and it doesn't feel that different, but it certainly seems to be going a little bit quicker, and that's always a good thing."

Overtaking is expected to be especially difficult around the Hungaroring this year.

In Miami an excess of caution on McLaren's part about the potential of rain allowed Mercedes to pit Antonelli before Norris and leap into the lead.

Norris' pole provides an opportunity to make amends for that - if he can keep Leclerc behind on the run to the first corner.

After winning two consecutive constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025, as well as Norris' drivers' championship last year, McLaren have not had a great season at the start of this new regulation cycle.

Securing the title against a late-season onslaught from Max Verstappen and Red Bull put them behind on designing this year's car, and they took some missteps on aerodynamic philosophy that only became fully understood after the first handful of races.

An upgrade package introduced by McLaren this weekend, their first since Miami, is the fruit of work aimed at correcting course, and the first signs are positive.

They have also struggled to get on top of the operation of the new Mercedes engine, feeling for the first time that they were suffering for not being a works partner of a manufacturer.

"It's just nice to be on pole," said Norris, who had also shown competitive pace in Belgium last weekend but was denied a good result by a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts, and then by bad luck with the timing of a safety car.

"I have felt good all weekend. The last few weekends, honestly, I felt pretty good and it's been nice I continued my good feelings in the car.

"I had my money on Ferrari before the weekend and they have been insanely quick, but, come qualifying, we just seemed to take more of a step forward. I knew it was possible and that has been a good feeling - and one that I have missed for quite a while."

As for his prospects in the race, Norris alluded to strong performances from the Mercedes and Ferrari drivers on the race-simulation runs in Friday practice when he said: "The race pace on others looked very strong. It is always a bit tricky to know how things will go with a new car and new bits."

Leclerc, though, felt Norris would certainly be in the fight, and both have some protection from Hamilton and Antonelli, both demoted by three-place penalties to fifth and seventh respectively.

"Lando seems to be very, very strong, so I'll say Lando [is favourite]," Leclerc said. "But if you look over the course of the season, Mercedes has always been up there, so I do not doubt that they'll all be in the fight as well."

Norris takes pole as Hamilton given grid penalty

Malaysia set to host postponed Bahrain GP

At Aston Martin there was at last some reason to feel positive after a dark time this season.

So much had been expected of the team when design legend Adrian Newey joined in March last year, but a late start to their design process, combined with engine partner Honda falling well short of performance and - like McLaren - some errors in philosophy, have left them cemented at the back all year.

In absolute terms, progressing beyond the first session for the first time all season, and lining up 16th, is nothing special. But to be able to compete with other teams, for pretty much the first time all year, was a major step.

In percentage terms, this was not quite Aston Martin's best performance of the season - they were 0.012% closer to pole in Japan. But it is huge compared with where they have fallen since as others have developed their cars.

There is a Honda engine upgrade to come for the next race after the summer break - of undefined size. More importantly, this has revitalised faith in Aston Martin's development capabilities after three years of upgrades that failed to deliver what the team expected.

"There is more potential to unlock in the car, but it's normal when you have such a big package," Alonso said.

"It was important for everyone in the team as it has been a tough period in both factories.

"Having the deficit that we had in terms of performance in the first half of the year and this package, it didn't change many positions, but it changed a lot the momentum of everyone in the factory.

"It's not any more that we are chasing something that we don't know. We know exactly what we are looking for and we know exactly the targets for the next package or the targets for next year. So that's for me the biggest change of this weekend."

Whether it is enough for Alonso to decide to commit to another season behind the wheel remains to be seen.

He turns 45 next week. He has said he still feels competitive - and continues to prove it. But he is no fan of the energy management required from this year's engines.

He continues to profess his confidence that Newey and Honda will eventually produce the best car and engine. But, as he keeps repeating, the question is how long that will take, and whether it fits his timeline.

As he said upon arriving in Hungary on Thursday: "It's not a problem with the competitiveness of the team. It's just a problem of whether Formula 1 gives me the adrenaline that I need to live."

Alonso has a lot of thinking to do as he heads off on his summer break - his first as a father - next week.

title: Ramsay-Peaty in tears after missing out on gold again
description: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty questions how his future looks after missing out on gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.

It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it.

"I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard," the Englishman said after taking 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games, his eyes and cheeks red with emotion.

"It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much."

Ramsay-Peaty has done it all in this sport.

Three Olympic gold medals. Eight world titles. The 14 fastest times in history.

But after taking a break from swimming amid a wave of mental health issues in 2023, he is still searching for that winning feeling again on the big stage.

He was pipped to Olympic gold in Paris two years ago. In Glasgow, despite coming into the final as the fastest qualifier, he had to settle for bronze.

He was beaten by Australia's Sam Williamson but also Jersey's history-maker Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old he has taken under his wing.

Ramsay-Peaty was third at halfway and could not close the gap. His time - 59.65 seconds - was more than four-tenths slower than his semi-final swim and three seconds off his personal best from seven years ago.

"It took a lot of courage to get back into the sport, so we should be happy with everything we get, but then that contradicts the athlete inside me and what I work for," he said.

"I just think I deserve more. I know sport isn't about what you deserve or even what you work for - it's who gets it on the day.

"I just know I'm a better athlete than that. It's very disappointing."

Ramsay-Peaty has spoken about the difficult decisions that come with being an elite athlete. The time away from his son, whom he held in his arms after the Paris silver. The events at home he has to miss.

"They are not even sacrifices; they are choices," he said.

"It's like getting knocked out in the group stages in the World Cup for a very good team. You know you're better and it hurts because you know you have to wait for a very long time for the next championships.

"This is probably - realistically - my last Commonwealth Games and I thought I'd trained for better. I could do better. I've been faster this season. That's where the frustration is."

Ramsay-Peaty has made no secret of the fact he is still competing in the quest for Olympic gold.

He considered retirement again after Paris, but committed to another four years when the 50m race was added to programme for Los Angeles 2028.

This 100m breaststroke is his event - the one in which he went unbeaten in eight years - but there may be a time when he has to let it go.

The 50m race - a dash down one length of the pool - would be less taxing on the body, and Ramsay-Peaty is due back in the pool for that event on Sunday morning.

"Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know," he said.

"When it hurts like this, the 50 is probably my super strength with my power.

"With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell.

"I just feel like I couldn't have given more this cycle. If I had given less, would it have even equalled more?"

Given the emotion, there are times you wonder how close Ramsay-Peaty is to walking away entirely.

He appeared to walk to the edge but always turned back, insisting the drive for LA remains.

"I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight.

"It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

title: Joshua knocked down twice as dramatic win sets up Fury fight
description: Anthony Joshua suffers two knockdowns before recovering to dramatically stop Kristian Prenga in the second round.
fullText:
Anthony Joshua suffered two knockdowns - the first happening after just 20 seconds - before recovering to dramatically stop Kristian Prenga in the second round of his comeback fight in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The British heavyweight was fighting for the first time since surviving the December car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele.

He was sensationally rocked by a huge uppercut from underdog Prenga in the opening round, and then hit the canvas again later in the round.

At that point he looked on the verge of one of the biggest shock defeats in heavyweight history, with the long-awaited Tyson Fury fight hanging by a thread.

But Joshua produced one of the greatest escapes of his career, and now that fight is on.

He unleashed his right hand in the second round, with the final shot sending Albanian Prenga crashing down and forcing the referee to halt the contest.

"It's more than punch power. That was spirit, that was Latz, that was Sina, that was the families. It hurts to even talk about it. It has been tough," Joshua, 36, said.

He choked up and stepped away from the microphone, before adding: "It's my brothers. I don't want to talk about it."

There had been speculation fellow Briton Fury might make a appearance despite insisting he would not attend.

But the master of mind games stayed true to his word, with Fury nowhere to be seen barely 24 hours on from his own warm-up win over Mariusz Wach in Thailand.

"I respect everything he has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we're here now. I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat," Joshua said about the prospect of fighting Fury.

Contracts have been signed, but the venue and date for a fight more than a decade in the making are still unknown.

This chaotic night, however, belonged to Joshua in a victory forged through adversity during the most difficult months of his life.

Relive Joshua's dramatic comeback knockout win

Bloodied Kelly battles past Agyarko to retain title

Given the circumstances, this was never going to be a straightforward return for Joshua. Few, however, could have predicted the drama that unfolded inside six minutes.

Joshua carried the names of Ghami and Ayodele on his chest and walked to the ring alongside his entire team in a quiet show of unity. The canvas carried their names too, alongside the words 'My Brother's Keeper'.

His comeback could scarcely have begun in any worse fashion. Just 20 seconds in, a right uppercut from Prenga sent Joshua crashing to the canvas and stunned the arena.

Joshua smiled as he climbed to his feet. Prenga, who arrived with 20 knockouts from his 20 victories but little profile even with boxing's hardcore followers, sensed an opportunity.

Promoter Eddie Hearn barked instructions from ringside, while Joshua stablemate Oleksandr Usyk watched on with a look of concern.

A left uppercut later in the round dumped Joshua on the canvas again. He was still unsteady at the start of the second round and appeared to be there for the taking, but Prenga surprisingly began to box off the back foot and let the Watford fighter off the hook.

Joshua capitalised and using his years of experience - and perhaps the emotion - he drew Prenga on to a jab before uncorking a crushing right hand. More rights followed as Prenga collapsed to the canvas and the referee had seen enough.

This was 35-year-old Prenga's second loss in his career.

It was Joshua's first test against a recognised professional opponent since Daniel Dubois stopped him in September 2024.

His only fight since had come against YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul in December, 10 days before the fatal crash that left him injured.

Joshua passed the Prenga test, but not in the manner anyone expected. It was not the destructive, free-flowing champion who once swept opponents aside.

After defeating 46-year-old Wach in Pattaya, the question of whether Fury would show up to watch Joshua became a subplot of fight night.

A Fury lookalike briefly fooled reporters when he stepped out of a taxi, while Fury's manager Spencer Brown insisted the 'Gypsy King' would be "there in spirit".

The fight between two of the most recognisable names in British boxing is understood to have been agreed for November.

Neither man is at the peak of his powers, but while the commercial appeal remains strong, Joshua's struggles are likely to leave Fury a clear favourite.

The bout is expected to stream on Netflix. British fans are hoping for a homecoming event, but it is understood Saudi organisers and broadcasters favour a venue in the United States to cater for American audiences.

"We've signed the contract. Everything is done," Hearn said.

"But tonight wasn't about Tyson Fury. It was about the strength Anthony Joshua has shown just to be here.

"No-one knows what he's been through over the last seven months. When he went down in the first round, I thought he'd come back too soon."

title: Littler sets up Price final at World Matchplay
description: Luke Littler is on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament average record after another impressive victory saw him reach the final.
fullText:
Defending champion Luke Littler strolled into the World Matchplay final with a 17-5 demolition of unseeded Dirk van Duijvenbode in Blackpool.

The world number one raced in an 8-2 advantage and was averaging 117.10 and on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament match average record of 114.99

Littler admitted afterwards that distracted him and his level did drop slightly as he finished with an average just below 111.

However, that leaves him well placed to beat Taylor's tournament average of 106.31, with Littler's currently at 110.88.

The teenager's victory also means he has now amassed more than £3m in the PDC's order of merit, and is more than £2m clear of world number two Luke Humphries.

Littler will face Wales' Gerwyn Price in Sunday's final after he beat Netherlands' Gian van Veen 17-10.

Sunday's final gets under way at 20:05 BST, with the Women's World Matchplay taking place in the afternoon session from 13:00 – Beau Greaves and defending champion Lisa Ashton the top two seeds.

Littler has averaged more than 109 in all four matches in this year's tournament as he looks to join Taylor and Michael van Gerwen as the only back-to-back winners of the Matchplay.

The run is also continuing his sublime form in longer-format matches - this win extending the streak to 28 successive wins in games with 20 or more legs.

His last defeat over a match of that duration was when he burst on to the scene in the 2024 World Championship and lost to Luke Humphries in the final.

That gives an indication of the challenge that Price will face on Sunday in his second Matchplay final.

The pair have a bit of rivalry with Price's on-stage roars and antics often provoking Littler into doing similar, but the teenager denied that Price can get "under his skin".

Earlier in the week, Price said that some players can "make it too easy" for Littler.

Despite their battles, Littler has won the past nine encounters between the pair, with Price's last success in their opening meeting of 2026.

The Welshman has never beat Littler in a game that has contained more than 15 legs so will have to reach new heights in the best-of-35 final.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Littler said: "Me and Gez always have great games. Gez will want to try and get me into a roaring battle. As long as I can get into the lead that will be the thing."

Price broke in the opening leg of the game and charged into a 4-1 lead, before a scrappy run of legs saw both players break throw regularly to leave Price leading 11-9 at the final mini-break.

From there, the seventh seed powered on and stretched away from Van Veen in scoring and finishing to seal a comfortable victory.

Both players missed 23 darts at a double across the match, while Van Veen was broken nine times in 14 legs throwing first on what was a difficult night for the world number three.

The victory sees Price climb to fourth in the order of merit, above Jonny Clayton, and in turn becomes Welsh number one.

Price told Sky Sports he was "happy" to reach the final, but "getting one up" on good friend Clayton was his main focus going into the tie.
